area.summary: A filled trace shows how a measurement changes across an ordered interval while keeping its baseline in view.
area.useWhen: Track a volume or level over time, or give forecasts and reference ranges a distinct visual region.
area.data: Supply ordered categories and nullable numeric series, or rows with a label and numeric value. Overlay examples use fields such as forecast, referenceLow, referenceHigh, and highlight.
area.reading: Follow the upper edge for the measurement. Read patterned or shaded bands against their boundary labels and the vertical scale.
notes: Use a complete sequence of increasing ISO timestamps for elapsed-time spacing in time-aware variants.
Set reference bounds and forecast boundaries explicitly when using these variants for your own data.

bar.summary: Bars make quantities comparable through their length from a common baseline.
bar.useWhen: Compare totals by product, machine, or shift. Use grouped bars for side-by-side series and stacked bars for contributions to a total.
bar.data: Supply categories with named numeric series or rows with label and value. A null sample is unavailable and zero remains a valid value.
bar.reading: Compare lengths using the same baseline. In signed stacks, compare positive and negative contributions on their respective sides of zero.
notes: Horizontal bars give long category names more room.

line.summary: A line connects ordered observations so direction, rate of change, and interruptions can be inspected.
line.useWhen: Track temperature over a shift, compare multiple signals, or inspect excursions against a threshold.
line.data: Supply categories and named nullable numeric series, or rows with label and value. Some variants use row fields such as low, high, threshold, goal, forecast, or events.
line.reading: Check the time axis before interpreting slope. Inspect missing samples and use a brush or zoom when a dense trace obscures short excursions.
notes: Large Data spaces readings by sample index even when labels are ISO dates.
The Fixed Scale example retains its 0–120 axis.

scatter.summary: A scatter plot places each observation at the intersection of two measurements.
scatter.useWhen: Look for correlations, clusters, gaps, and outliers in paired readings such as pressure and flow.
scatter.data: Supply rows with numeric x and y coordinates, with optional group and label. Supplied series use the sample position for x.
scatter.reading: Read both axes together. In the Jitter example, the horizontal offset separates overlapping marks around their original position.
notes: Use Large Data to inspect dense datasets. It shows density when zoomed out.

candlestick.summary: Each candle summarizes an interval with its opening value, closing value, lowest reading, and highest reading.
candlestick.useWhen: Show how price or another sampled measure moved within consistent time intervals.
candlestick.data: Provide one row per interval with finite open, high, low, and close values. Use a date or category to label each interval.
candlestick.reading: The body spans open to close and the wick spans low to high. Check the color convention and the time interval before comparing candles.
notes: A value-only series derives approximate candle bounds. Supply complete rows when actual highs and lows matter.
Range and Crosshair illustrate different ways to inspect the same four values.

composed.summary: A composed plot aligns different marks, such as bars and a line, along a shared horizontal axis.
composed.useWhen: Compare actuals with a target, or inspect price and volume for the same market interval.
composed.data: Supply aligned categories and series in the order used by the chosen example. Price Volume also reads open, high, low, close, and volume from rows.
composed.reading: Identify which marks belong to each series and check each vertical axis before comparing changes between measures.
notes: Grouped and Stacked combine bars differently while keeping the overlaid trace.
Supply every series the selected variant expects. Missing series can pick up the included sample values.

live-line.summary: A live trace appends incoming measurements to a bounded history so the most recent activity stays in view.
live-line.useWhen: Watch a changing signal such as a sensor reading or request rate while a process runs.
live-line.data: Provide a stable liveStream with a subscribe function that returns cleanup. Send timestamped batches in nondecreasing Unix millisecond order. A reading may have a null value.
live-line.reading: Check the time window and units. Pause the view to inspect an interval while new readings continue to be retained.
notes: Capacity defaults to 4,096 readings.

gantt.summary: Horizontal task bars show scheduled start and end dates, and connectors show which work depends on other tasks.
gantt.useWhen: Plan a build, deployment, or maintenance window with overlapping work and handoffs.
gantt.data: Supply named task rows with numeric day offsets or ISO calendar dates for start and end. Use dependencies for multiple predecessors and progressPercent for completion percentages.
gantt.reading: Read duration across the timeline and follow the direction of dependency connectors. Milestones represent specific dates.
notes: Use one date convention for a schedule and give tasks stable IDs when using named dependencies.
Phase rows can group related tasks and label their timeline bands.

waterfall.summary: Floating bars show how successive gains and losses move a running balance from an opening point to a closing value.
waterfall.useWhen: Explain a budget bridge, cash-flow change, or the drivers of a difference between two totals.
waterfall.data: Supply one numeric series of ordered changes. Aligned rows can mark checkpoints with total or subtotal set to true.
waterfall.reading: Read the endpoints for the running balance and the bar lengths for individual changes. A total bar reads from the baseline.
notes: Cash Flow displays the input amounts directly. Other variants label each input unit as one million dollars.

lollipop.summary: A stem and end marker encode a single magnitude for each category with a small visual footprint.
lollipop.useWhen: Compare a list of categories where direct labels and the exact endpoints are helpful.
lollipop.data: Provide categories and one numeric series. Supply precomputed signed differences in percentage points for the Change example.
lollipop.reading: Compare the end markers to the common baseline. Use horizontal orientation when labels need more space.
notes: Horizontal uses a fixed 0–100 percent scale. Change uses a fixed −3 to 3 percentage-point scale.

dumbbell.summary: Two markers and the line between them show a paired comparison for each category.
dumbbell.useWhen: Compare before and after readings, two versions, or actual and target values for the same items.
dumbbell.data: Supply categories and two aligned numeric series in the order the endpoints should be read. Each displayed pair needs two finite values.
dumbbell.reading: The markers are the two measurements and the span is their difference. Use the legend to identify the starting and ending values.
notes: The default chart displays seconds on a fixed 0.5–4 scale. Vertical formats values in U.S. dollars.

uncertainty.summary: Intervals around a point estimate show how much uncertainty surrounds a measurement or prediction.
uncertainty.useWhen: Compare effects with a forest plot or show upper and lower bounds around a forecast.
uncertainty.data: Supply estimates as rows with value, low, and high, plus an optional label. Ribbon examples can also read innerLow and innerHigh.
uncertainty.reading: Read the estimate at the center and the uncertainty at the interval endpoints. In a forest plot, check which intervals cross the reference line.
notes: Calculate the bounds before passing them in and specify what confidence or coverage they represent.

bump.summary: A bump chart follows each item's rank across successive periods.
bump.useWhen: Show which teams, products, or metrics moved up or down a leaderboard over time.
bump.data: Supply period categories and one numeric series per item. The chart derives ranks from the values at each period.
bump.reading: Read positions as ranks. Use the individual values to judge the size of a change between periods.
notes: Use the Ascending variant when a smaller value should rank ahead of a larger one.

slope.summary: Lines between two endpoints show the direction and size of change for each item.
slope.useWhen: Compare two meaningful snapshots, such as latency before and after a rollout.
slope.data: Supply two ordered categories and one aligned numeric series per item. Use consistent units for the two values.
slope.reading: Read the labeled endpoint values and follow the line for direction. Crossings show changes in relative order.
notes: The Response Time variant treats a decrease as an improvement.

sparkline.summary: A compact trace places a short history beside a headline metric, table row, or small multiple.
sparkline.useWhen: Show recent direction and volatility where a full chart would take attention away from the primary number.
sparkline.data: Provide ordered categories and named numeric series. Use null for missing readings. The Stat Card example can read rows.previous for a prior-period comparison.
sparkline.reading: Look at direction, gaps, and the latest value. Use a larger plot with an explicit scale when you need exact comparisons.
notes: Synced links sample inspection across multiple traces.
Range lets the reader narrow the visible history.

heatmap.summary: A calendar heatmap shows how the intensity of a daily measure changes across weeks and months.
heatmap.useWhen: Find recurring activity, quiet periods, and unusually busy days in a count or other nonnegative measure.
heatmap.data: Provide dated rows with date and value, or a numeric series aligned to date categories. The chart sums repeated dates into UTC days.
heatmap.reading: Read the weekday and month for position, then use the legend for intensity. Inspect a cell for its exact date and value.
notes: Negative values are clamped to zero for this calendar model.
The Scroll example keeps weekday labels visible while moving through the calendar.

diverging.summary: A diverging stack lays opposing responses on either side of a common center.
diverging.useWhen: Compare the distribution of answers to survey questions that share the same ordered response scale.
diverging.data: Supply one category per question and one numeric series per response level in scale order. Name the neutral series Neutral.
diverging.reading: Compare the shares on either side of the center and check the count behind each percentage in the inspection panel.
notes: The chart normalizes nonnegative counts within each category and splits Neutral across the center when present.

stream.summary: A streamgraph uses stacked bands to show changing composition across a sequence.
stream.useWhen: Look for the rise and fall of multiple contributors such as traffic sources or production lines.
stream.data: Supply ordered categories and numeric series. Missing readings count as zero in the stack and appear as a dash in inspection.
stream.reading: Read a band's thickness for its contribution. The moving baseline in the Default view serves the layout. Expand shows each category as 100%.
notes: Use nonnegative quantities when comparing shares in Expand.
Default and Loading use D3 inside-out order and wiggle stacking.

histogram.summary: A histogram counts how many observations fall within each interval of a numeric scale.
histogram.useWhen: Find common ranges, tails, or possible groups in measurements such as cycle times.
histogram.data: Provide raw numeric samples by series or rows with value and an optional group. The chart chooses bins across the supplied range.
histogram.reading: Read the horizontal interval and its vertical frequency. Check the bin widths and group sizes before comparing shapes.
notes: Overlay retains separate series. Stacked shows their combined frequency per interval.

ridgeline.summary: Overlapping density curves compare the shapes of several numeric distributions on one horizontal scale.
ridgeline.useWhen: Compare where measurements cluster across months, regions, or equipment groups.
ridgeline.data: Supply numeric samples per group with series, or rows with value and an optional group. Each group produces its own estimated curve.
ridgeline.reading: Compare the location, spread, and number of peaks. Interpret the smooth curve as an estimate of density.
notes: Use the same measurement units across groups.

ecdf.summary: An empirical cumulative distribution shows the fraction of observations at or below each value.
ecdf.useWhen: Compare service levels, percentiles, or the share of jobs that meet a time target.
ecdf.data: Supply raw numeric samples per series, or rows with value and an optional group. The chart sorts the samples before calculating cumulative shares.
ecdf.reading: At a chosen value, read up to the curve to find the share that meets it. Read across from a percentile to find its measured threshold.
notes: Large steps can indicate repeated values.
Use Compare to read two distributions on the same scale.

beeswarm.summary: A beeswarm keeps each observation visible by spreading nearby points along a secondary direction.
beeswarm.useWhen: Show cluster density and outliers while retaining the individual readings within each group.
beeswarm.data: Supply raw numeric samples per series, or rows with value and an optional group. The renderer positions markers from those samples.
beeswarm.reading: Read value along the measurement axis. The perpendicular spread separates marks and helps show where observations concentrate.
notes: The Vertical variant rotates the measurement axis.
